name: Olga Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Olga, 27, with a vocational cooking certificate and the evening line to run. I check deliveries and allergy tickets, then cook fish while two junior cooks watch the pans. I love a clean service, but the low rate and late bus leave little after rent.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is work and home like outside the rush?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone, have no children and have less than a month's bills saved. There are few other lead-cook openings nearby. I use AI every day for a first draft of nameless stock counts, then check every quantity against the actual delivery slips myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AI Plateau won't change who stands over the hot pans. The new ordering screen might save us a little counting, but a cook still has to taste the sauce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the evening line and I'm good at it, but my rate is low and I've saved less than a month's bills. If Friday covers are poor, the owner trims my shifts before any machine does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This November I'll keep running the hot line and ask the owner for next month's rota in writing. In the plateau’s first year I’ll save some cleared extra-shift pay left after rent, food and the bus toward a separate two-month bills reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy about our thin margin, though the cooking itself feels solid. A quiet dining room worries me more than the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the money get tight first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent is due three days after payday, so a lost Friday shift goes straight through my little reserve. I won't buy a new knife just to feel prepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the screen's food information?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check every printed allergy ticket against the guest's actual order before anything touches a pan. The screen doesn't know whether a spoon crossed into the wrong sauce.

I'd say the **ordering screen** may save counting, while I still have to taste the sauce.
think: My **low rate** and short reserve make lost Friday shifts painful already.
I trust my **cooking skill**, but a quiet dining room could still cut my hours.
do: Keep **the hot line** and ask for next month's written rota.
Save **cleared extra-shift pay** left after rent, food and bus toward a two-month bills reserve.
feel: I feel **anxious** about realistic lost shifts despite confidence at the stove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the owner Steady Disruption can draft orders and a rota, but it can't plate a hot fish safely. I'd ask the crew to check the supplier list and every allergy note before service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cheap planner could make the owner squeeze prep hours, and my low wage has no padding. I'm curious about useful tools, but I won't let generated allergy advice reach a plate unchecked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll show the junior cook how to check an AI draft against the actual supplier label and the guest ticket, with me signing off. I'll ask the owner to keep the paid prep hours on the rota; if they are cut, I'll seek a posted paid lead-cook opening accepting my cooking certificate and experience, and leave only for a signed offer whose net pay after travel replaces my full current weekly take-home and its hours fit the late bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That makes me anxious, not helpless. I know the pans and the team. Our rent doesn't accept a clever rota instead of wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The junior cook starts with sesame and nut labels, because the printout can be confidently wrong. I'd stand beside them until they can verify the packet and the guest ticket without guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for any lead title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a title with fewer paid prep hours is a pay cut. I'd keep my current shifts until the other restaurant confirms the wage, hours and journey in writing.

I'd ask the **crew** to verify supplier labels and allergy tickets before service.
think: A cheaper **planner** could reduce my paid preparation hours despite my strong kitchen skills.

do: Check **AI drafts** against supplier labels and guest tickets under my supervision.

feel: I feel **anxious** about wages but capable of checking the new workflow.

fieldNote: Her **AI use** stays behind human checks of allergens and actual supplier packets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2028 can do our ordering and plans, but hands-on cooking robots aren't on this card until about 2031. I'd ask for paid shifts and proper allergy checks, not a machine promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owner might slash the planning and prep time I get paid for before a robot lifts a pan. With less than a month's reserve, a big cut would keep me awake; I cannot wait until 2031 to count the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd document my paid prep and service hours and ask the owner what changes in 2028. In the first year after AGI arrives, I'd keep cooking while the hours hold; if the owner cuts them, I'd apply for a posted hospital kitchen lead role only if my certificate and experience meet its rules, and move only after a signed offer replaces my full current weekly take-home after travel, the late bus works, and safe food training is paid without losing current wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the chance of a big cut to prep pay, though I am still sleeping. I know how to keep people fed safely while the hours remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a hospital kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Its meals still need people who can control allergens and hot equipment, at least until capable robots arrive around 2031. I don't know whether there will be a paid opening, so the vacancy has to be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the offer never comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep the restaurant shifts that remain and cut the new equipment purchase. I won't borrow against an imaginary hospital wage.

say: I'd tell the **crew** that AGI changes plans by 2028 while capable cooking robots follow around 2031.
I'd ask for **paid shifts** and verified allergy checks during that gap.
think: A possible **prep-hour cut** could take a large part of my low pay before robots arrive.
My **short reserve** makes the rent sums worrying now.
do: Record **paid prep hours** and request the owner's 2028 staffing plan.
Apply **posted paid hospital cook** after cuts if certificate/experience accepted; require paid safe-food training without wage loss.
Keep **current shifts** until signed full-weekly-net replacement offer after travel with workable late bus.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible large pay cut while I can still act.
S2.quote: I cannot wait until 2031 to count the rent.
fieldNote: A **possible prep cut** creates realistic income risk, but she does not yet expect a big loss or report broken sleep.
A **hospital move** needs a real vacancy, accepted certificate, safe paid training and signed net replacement pay.

steps.text: Record paid prep and service hours and ask for the 2028 staffing plan

Require paid food-safety training without current wage loss and workable late bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the kitchen AGI by 2031 gives us five years to prepare, with hands-on robots around 2034. We should make the allergy records and training worth paying people for, not pretend software can touch every plate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me build a case for a proper paid food-safety lead post, but it doesn't create one. The owner could still trim my rate now, so I need an actual vacancy and money in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask whether the restaurant will fund the recognised food-safety supervisor course on paid time, keeping my cooking wages and shifts. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for a actual posted paid safety-lead job only after the course is accepted and completed; I'd keep my line job until a signed net offer after travel replaces my full current weekly take-home and the route fits late service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because five years isn't a guarantee of a wage. It does give me enough time to train without making a desperate jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for that course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot pay for the food-safety course from the rent envelope. I'd enroll only with a funded place, paid study time and a certificate that an actual posted paid employer accepts alongside my cooking qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the restaurant declines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I continue leading service and use the supplier checks I know. I don't spend my rent on a course with no accepted credential or paid opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2036 gives a long lead, but the restaurant must pay for every safe shift now. Cooking robots might come around 2039, and nobody should sell us a training poster as a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I could be leading food safety across kitchens, or still earning this low rate at the stove. Ten years helps if paid posts and recognised training actually exist; my rent is due this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the line's allergy log accurate and save a share of cleared extra-shift pay left after rent, food and bus toward two months' bills. In the first year after 2036 I'd renew my cooking work while it pays, and seek a posted food-safety lead role only if my certificate and experience qualify, the written net wage after travel replaces my full current weekly take-home, and I can get home after the late shift; I'd leave only with a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distance, but anxious about the thin reserve today. A decade does not fill a rent envelope on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might happen before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering and rosters might change before 2036, but a hot fryer and an allergy mistake are physical risks now. I would keep supervising those checks while anybody pays me to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the decade useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid route into food safety and enough extra shifts to save would make it useful. A glossy certificate that employers reject would only cost me time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a fast cut in paid prep would beat my savings. Written shifts and a genuine paid safety course would help, followed by a real job offer that covers the journey.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs off an allergy ticket when software makes a confident mistake. A safe meal has someone's name on it, and that person needs paid time.

headlineQuote: A safe meal has someone's name on it, and that person needs paid time.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old certified cook** who leads a busy evening line and checks allergy tickets before plates leave.
Her **strong practical skill** earns a low rate; less than a month saved makes reduced prep hours a real risk.
She uses **AI tools daily** but keeps supplier labels, guest tickets and hot-equipment safety under a cook's supervision.
Across faster scenarios she seeks **paid safety training** and a real qualified post, while retaining wages until a signed offer.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI picture** could cut paid preparation hours before cooking robots appear around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **written paid shifts**, funded recognised safety training and a signed replacement wage after travel.
